summary:
Sections 153 to 155 of Kiribati's Penal Code criminalise sex between men. Anal intercourse carries up to fourteen years' imprisonment, attempts and assault with intent to commit it up to seven years, and acts of gross indecency between males up to five years. Sex between women is not an offence.

The provisions are not enforced. A 2015 US State Department human rights report recorded no prosecutions under them, and no prosecution of an LGBTQ person under these sections has been reported.

The same 2015 report recorded no societal discrimination or violence based on sexual orientation. That observation is a decade old and the inventory holds no later survey of the social climate.

No constitutional or statutory non-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity generally. Article 15(3) of the Constitution bars discrimination by reference to race, place of origin, political opinions, colour and creed. Gender discrimination is prohibited only in employment, a limit the 2015 State Department report described as poorly enforced.

The Employment and Industrial Relations Code 2015, Article 107(2)(b), has prohibited employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2015. The article does not name gender identity.

The Marriage Act (Cap 54) does not expressly bar recognition of a marriage between partners of the same sex. It assumes that the partners are of opposite sex, and its restrictions on marriage cover relatives, parties below the age of 16, and bigamy.

At the 21st-session Universal Periodic Review, France, Slovenia and Chile urged Kiribati to decriminalise homosexuality. The Kiribati delegation made no response to those recommendations. It stated that it was considering Uruguay's advice to adopt legislation prohibiting discrimination covering gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation.

In November 2016 Kiribati voted at the UN General Assembly against an amendment that would have defunded the mandate of the Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The amendment was rejected 84-77, and Kiribati and Sri Lanka were the only countries then criminalising homosexuality that voted to retain the mandate.
tangentialFactors:
A November 2016 report on the General Assembly vote cited Kiribati, together with Sri Lanka, as one of two countries then maintaining anti-homosexuality laws. It is dated evidence that sections 153 to 155 remained on the statute book at that point.

The Constitution restricts land ownership to I-Kiribati. This is a general citizenship-based restriction rather than a gender-identity rule, but it illustrates how narrowly Article 15(3) frames protected grounds.

Research on gender and sexual diversity in the Pacific, including Besnier's 2014 study 'Gender on the edge', documents a Pinapinaaine or Binabinaaine gender role in Kiribati and Tuvalu that Western vocabulary would label homosexual or transgender. A gender-diverse visitor's presentation may therefore be read against a locally recognised category rather than a Western one, though the sources describe cultural roles and not legal status.
localsOnly:
For I-Kiribati residents, sections 153 to 155 of the Penal Code remain the operative sexual-offence provisions, with penalties of up to fourteen, seven and five years as set out above. The 2015 State Department report recorded no prosecutions, so the exposure is legal rather than documented enforcement.

Workplace protection is the one area where sexual orientation is a named ground: Article 107(2)(b) of the Employment and Industrial Relations Code 2015 has applied since 2015. Gender discrimination is prohibited only in employment, and the 2015 report judged that prohibition poorly enforced. Outside employment there is no statutory protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Article 15(3) of the Constitution gives residents a non-discrimination guarantee limited to race, place of origin, political opinions, colour and creed. Sexual orientation and gender identity are not among the listed grounds.

The Marriage Act (Cap 54) regulates marriage without addressing same-sex unions directly; its substantive restrictions concern relatives, parties under 16 and bigamy. Land ownership is reserved to I-Kiribati under the Constitution.

The government told the Universal Periodic Review that it was considering anti-discrimination legislation covering gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the anti-discrimination legislation flagged at the 21st-session Universal Periodic Review was ever enacted is unresolved. No source in the inventory records its adoption or its failure.

The most recent legal-status evidence in the inventory dates from 2016. Whether sections 153 to 155 remain unamended, and whether enforcement policy has changed since, is not sourced.

No post-2015 measurement of social climate, reported discrimination or reported violence against LGBTQ people appears in the inventory. The 2015 State Department observation of no reported societal discrimination or violence cannot be treated as current.

One source asserts that lesbians may face violence and discrimination, but cites no incident, date or underlying record. That claim is unresolved and is not carried as a finding.

The inventory addresses sexual orientation far more than gender identity. Legal recognition of a trans person's gender, document and marker rules, entry screening, and access to gender-affirming care are not sourced for Kiribati, and no assessment of them is possible from these materials.
